caption:
OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team and moved the researchers into its main research and Applied groups, Fortune reports.
The reason: its general model GPT-6 Astra did better at robot tasks than specialized robot AI in an Nvidia study.
OpenAI says it is not giving up on robots. Sam Altman is aiming for a first humanoid demo in 2027.

Can one general AI really run every robot?

threads_text: OpenAI just disbanded its robotics team. Not because it quit robots, but because its general model GPT-6 Astra beat specialized robot AI in an Nvidia test, 74.8% to 51.0%. The catch is speed: over 13 seconds per step. Will one big model run every robot, or do robots need their own brains?

paragraphs.text: OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team and moved its researchers to other parts of the company, Fortune reported on November 13, 2026. OpenAI confirmed the reorganization when Fortune asked about it, and a spokesperson said robotics remains a core part of the company's long-term vision.

According to Fortune, the robotics research staff now sit inside OpenAI's main research team, which reports to Chief Research Officer Mark Chen. The applied robotics and hardware teams were placed in the larger Applied organization, which reports to OpenAI President Greg Brockman. Fortune did not report any layoffs.
Why OpenAI says it made the change

OpenAI told Fortune that at the start of the year its researchers expected the best route to robot intelligence to run through models such as Sora, its video generation model. Since then, the company said, its general purpose frontier models, including GPT-6 Astra, have shown they can be applied to robotics directly, and that finding drove the reorganization.

Outside research points the same way. In a study published on October 14, 2026, Nvidia's Seattle Robotics Lab tested GPT-6 Astra as a robot policy on RoboLab-120, a set of 120 simulated pick-and-place tasks with a robot arm and no robot-specific training. An agentic setup, in which Astra worked in a persistent Codex session, succeeded on 74.8% of the tasks. The strongest specialized model on the same leaderboard, Lakeside, reached 51.0%.

The same study shows the cost of that result. Nvidia measured about 13.4 seconds per call and roughly $36.40 in tokens per episode for the agentic setup, compared with well under a second per step for dedicated robot models. The authors named latency as a major barrier to real-world use.

This is not OpenAI's first change of course in robotics. The company wound down an earlier robotics team in 2020, rebuilt a stand-alone team in 2024 and partnered with the startup Figure on humanoid robot models, a deal that ended in February 2025 when Figure said it would build its own robot AI. Fortune reports OpenAI is now developing its own humanoid robot, and that Sam Altman is aiming for a first public demonstration in 2027.

Researchers quoted by Fortune were split on what the move means. Guanya Shi of Carnegie Mellon University said it suggests OpenAI no longer sees robotics as a special problem, but added that robots still need smaller models that run on board without a constant connection. MIT professor Russ Tedrake said robotics companies keep an advantage in deployment experience and site data.

The reorganization comes as OpenAI trims projects outside its core business. Fortune notes the company has dropped efforts including Sora to free up computing power, reportedly posted an operating loss of $10.9 billion in its most recent quarter, and is preparing for a possible public listing in early 2027.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the move is a bet that the same large model behind OpenAI's chat products can become the brain of a robot, rather than a separate system trained only on robot data. The Nvidia numbers support the accuracy side of that bet, while the speed and cost figures show why it is not yet practical outside a lab. It also puts pressure on robotics startups that raised money on the idea that robots need their own models.
The next test is the humanoid demonstration OpenAI is targeting for 2027, which will show whether a general model can control a physical robot fast enough to be useful.
